newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Samsung must discuss Fokker with Rabobank - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Samsung must discuss Fokker with Rabobank - analysts.

text.p: Analysts said on Wednesday South Korea's Samsung Aerospace should turn to Dutch Rabobank to acquire the knowledge they need to build new planes instead of acquiring the remains of bankrupt Fokker.
Rabobank picked up technology leases from Fokker in 1994 when Fokker was casting around for ways to raise cash.
Samsung is currently mulling over whether to buy the remnants of Fokker and the latest sticking point on Wednesday was reported to be the future of some 600 jobs at Fokker.

"Why buy some working plants, machines and few of the staff left? The more direct way would be to contact Rabobank to acquire the knowledge (for building aeroplanes)," said Andre Mulder at BZW in Amsterdam.
In the lease package is information on protypes for new aeroplanes, analysts said, as well as specifications related to the 70, 100 and 120-seater aircraft.

"It would take Samsung three to four years to develop new planes," said analyst Gert Jochems of NIBStrating. "They would be ahead of their (Chinese) competitors if they manage make use of the planes already developed by Fokker," he said.

Samsung would also be able to make use of the technical information that is currently in the hands of Rabobank, if it aqcuires Fokker, but it would boost operating expenses as it would have to pay for the information, analysts said.

Jochems said the Rabobank might have something like half a billion guilders in its drawer through the knowledge it leased from Fokker about two years ago, while in his view the remains of Fokker were only worth "some tens of millions of guilders".
A Rabobank spokesman declined to say whether Samsung had approached his company over the techno-leases.
Analysts said the chance that the deal between Samsung and the Dutch government would proceed was thin.
"It is not an industry any more, it's a few leftovers from a sector," said Mulder.

Analysts said Fokker, which went bankrupt in March, was almost stripped to the bones since engineering and services group Stork acquired the profitable maintenance division Fokker Aviation and most staff have left the firm or were made redundant when Fokker went bankrupt.
Since then several possible buyers have been circling Fokker, of which Samsung seemed most keen.

Earlier today, Dutch media reported that talks between Samsung and the Dutch government on the revival of bankrupt plane-maker Fokker were foundering on the issue of job security, although Dutch television reported last Sunday that negotiators from Samsung had reached broad agreement on the takeover.

Dutch Rabobank said the technical knowledge it leased from plane-maker Fokker in 1994 was not automatically for sale if the takeover talks with South Korea's Samsung Aerospace Industries come to a halt.
"The knowledge is there for a reviving of Fokker," said a Rabobank spokesman on Wednesday. "We have not put it in the shop-window."

The cooperative bank received tax benefits after the deal. The Dutch watchdog body on government spending said on Wednesday these considerably exceeded the 412 million guilders that had been injected into the Fokker capital through this transaction.
"Rabobank can compensate the costs on the deal with Fokker over some years," said the Rabobank spokesman. "We continue to depreciate this from our balance sheet," he said.
